@@123036206 <p> After the Albanese government spent half the parliamentary term promising to overhaul Australia 's government-run carbon neutral certification scheme -- data obtained by Tempests and Terawatts shows the Climate Active program is in a state of decline . <p> Climate Active , it appears , is being abandoned by corporate participants and the federal government alike , and with caretaker mode now in effect , the public remains in the dark as to what reforms the Albanese government may have made to the scheme . <p> atureLast week , to assess the current status of Australia 's carbon neutral certification scheme , I submitted a request to the Department of Climate Change , Energy , the Environment and Water ( DCCEEW ) for data on corporate participation under the Climate Active program . The data requested included the volume of emissions offset by each participant and the types of carbon credits used . <p> DCCEEW declined to provide the data in a useful format and instead pointed to the 540 individual reports -- all published in PDF format -- for the data about each entity that has obtained a @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ update to the same undertaking I completed in February 2023 and a link to the data from that exercise is available in the article I wrote at the time . <h> The high-level findings <p> As of March 2025 , there are 540 organisations , buildings , services , products or events that have current carbon neutral certifications under the carbon neutral program . <p> There are some interesting and some troubling trends in the data : <p> -- The total volume of emissions offset under Climate Active has fallen by around 10 per cent over the last two years . <p> -- Just three companies represent more than half of all emissions offset under the Climate Active scheme ; electricity retailers EnergyAustralia , Powershop and AGL Energy . <p> -- Participants in the program still overwhelmingly rely on cheaper international carbon credits to achieve carbon neutral certification . International units represent 89% of all offset credits used . <p> -- Concerningly , more than half ( 50.7% ) of offsets used by companies with active Climate Active certifications were Certified Emissions Reductions generated under the troubled Clean Development Mechanism @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ of many prominent brands , including several that had ranked amongst the top 10 largest offsetters in my 2023 analysis . This includes Telstra , the Brisbane City Council , Opal Australian Paper and Australia Post . <p> To its credit , Telstra announced its withdrawal from the Climate Active program alongside a commitment to make greater investments in directly reducing its emissions footprint , but many have withdrawn without making such commitments . <p> Other major brands have also withdrawn from the Climate Active program , including Afterpay , Jetstar , Ovo Energy and the federal government 's greenbank ; the Clean Energy Finance Corporation . <p> At a time when there is growing urgency and concern regarding the extent of corporate inaction in response to the climate crisis , falling participation in the Climate Active action could be cause for alarm . <p> But mounting evidence suggests that carbon offsetting regimes have done little to reduce emissions and have instead diverted investment away from more meaningful actions . So the exodus from the Climate Active program could also be indicative of the fact that the time to move @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ 2023 , recognising the need to evolve the program , Climate Active announced a review of its carbon neutral certification program via a statement titled ' We 're making changes ' . Within a week , Climate Active had published a consultation paper and called for submissions on how the program could be reshaped to modernise it and ' raise the level of climate ambition and action to get certified ' . <p> In the consultation paper , Climate Active flagged potential changes to the certification process , including restrictions on the types of international carbon offsets that could be used . In an acknowledgement of the flaws with carbon offsetting , Climate Active went so far as proposing to abandon and replace the ' carbon neutral ' terminology used by the scheme . <p> " The seventh proposal is to discontinue the term ' carbon neutral ' to describe the certified claim and to use a different term . The current trade mark would be discontinued and replaced with a new trade mark , adopting a new term . It is important the new term does not risk consumer @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ to be meaningful and reflect the achievements of participants through certification , " the consultation paper says . <p> The consultation paper was a positive indication that the Albanese government had taken seriously the concerns raised about the heavy reliance on carbon credits the scheme had encouraged , and the environmental integrity of carbon offsetting more generally . <p> However , that is where things stalled . <p> The last official update came in July 2024 , when Climate Active said it was considering the submissions it had received in response to the consultation paper , and that it anticipated that " an announcement about program reforms will be made later in 2024 " . <p> That announcement never came . <p> In response to my query about the status of the Climate Active program , a spokesperson for DCCEEW said " a decision about the future direction of the Climate Active program is yet to be made . " <p> " The Climate Active program continues to operate as usual , following the Climate Active Carbon Neutral Standard , " the spokesperson told Tempests and Terawatts . <p> " @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ the Climate Active program , including how to drive effective voluntary climate action and provide consumers with confidence about business ' climate claims . " <p> The Federal Government is now in caretaker mode and the fate of the Climate Active program ( and all of Australia 's federal climate policy ) now depends on the outcome of the federal election . <h> The problems with carbon offsetting <p> The problems with carbon offsetting are well documented . The problem is not so much with the underlying concept of offsetting -- there is perhaps a time and a place for emissions offsetting to aid the overall decarbonisation of particularly hard to abate industries . <p> However , the real-world use of carbon offsets has proven problematic . Rather than being used to account for the last remaining carbon after all reasonable efforts to reduce emissions have been exhausted -- the final tier of the greenhouse gas mitigation hierarchy -- programs like Climate Active incentivise the use of offsets to mitigate a company 's entire carbon footprint . <p> The fact that the Climate Active program is administered by the federal @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ the certifications it issues -- a certain level of heft . If it is good enough for the government , why should n't it be good enough for consumers and the courts ? <p> EnergyAustralia has made this argument in its defence to a greenwashing claim brought against it by the group Parents for Climate Action . The group has alleged that EnergyAustralia 's marketing of ' carbon neutral ' electricity and gas products is misleading and deceptive conduct , because the heavy reliance on carbon offsets means the products do not have a positive impact on the environment . <p> Hearings for Parents for Climate v EnergyAustralia will be held in May , and could have dramatic consequences for the Climate Active program -- and carbon offsetting more broadly -- if EnergyAustralia is found liable for greenwashing . @@123073775 <h> Opinion <h> Dutton wants to know if you 're better off now . It 's a trick question <h> Save articles for later <p> Add articles to your saved list and come back to them any time . <p> Advertisement <p> For most people , the simple answer to Peter Dutton 's repeated question -- are you better off today than you were three years ago ? -- is " no , I 'm not " . But if Dutton can convince us this is the key question we need to answer in this election , he 'll have conned us into giving him an easy run into government . <p> Why ? Because it 's the wrong question . It 's the question of a high-pressure salesman . A question that makes the problem seem a lot simpler than it is . A question for people who do n't like using their brain . <p> Illustration by Simon Letch <p> And it 's a question that points us away from the right question , which is : which of the two sides seems more likely to advance the @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ Economists have a concept called " sunk costs " -- money ( or time ) that you 've spent , and you ca n't unspend . Economics teaches an obvious lesson : you ca n't change the past , so forget it and focus on what you can change , the future . <p> But , since it 's become such a central issue in this election , let 's dissect Dutton 's magic question . For a start , it 's completely self-centred . Focus on what 's happened to you and your family and forget about what 's happened to anyone else . <p> Similarly , the implication is to focus on the monetary side of life . Forget about what 's happened to the natural environment , what we 've done to limit climate change , and what we 've done about intergenerational equity -- the way we rigged the system to favour the elderly at the expense of the young . <p> Next , Dutton 's question is quite subjective . He 's not asking us to do some calculations about our household budget or to @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ feel better or worse off . <p> Guess what ? This subjectivity makes us more likely to answer no . As we 've learnt from the psychologists , humans have evolved to remember bad events more strongly than good events . <p> This is why most people believe that inflation is much higher than the consumer price index tells us . As they do their weekly grocery shopping , they remember the price rises much more clearly than any price falls . And in the personal CPI they carry in their heads , they take no account of the many prices that did n't change -- which they should , and the real CPI does . <p> Advertisement <p> Humans find the bad more interesting and memorable than the good because the bad is more threatening , and we have evolved to search our environment for threats . <p> In this case , however , objective measurement confirms that most people are right in thinking their household budgets are harder to balance than they were three years ago . There are various ways to measure living standards , but probably @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ national household disposable income per person " . <p> Between June 2022 and March 2024 ( the latest quarter available ) , it fell by 3.6 per cent . It may have recovered a bit in the 12 months since then , but not by enough to stop it having fallen overall . <p> But that 's just an economy-wide average . We can break it down into more specific household categories . Those dependent on income from wages are worse off because consumer prices rose a little faster than wages -- though wage rises fell well short of price rises in the couple of years before Labor came to power . This is a shortfall wage-earning households would still be feeling in their efforts to balance their budgets . <p> The rise in interest rates since the last election means the households feeling by far the most pain over the past three years are those with mortgages . <p> This also means those who own their homes outright have felt the least pain . Most people on the age pension have done OK because most of them own their @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ rise in consumer prices . <p> Loading <p> As for the so-called self-funded retirees , they 've been laughing . Not only do they own their homes , their super and other investments earn more when interest rates are high . <p> True , it 's common for elections to be used to sack governments who 've presided over tough economic times . Be in power during a recession and you 're dead meat . So elections are often used to punish governments , on the rationale that the other lot could n't possibly be worse . <p> But the side that benefits from such circumstances , taking over when everything 's a mess , wo n't have it easy getting everyone back to work and having no trouble with the mortgage in just three years . <p> I can remember when the Morrison government was tossed out in 2022 , smarties among the Liberals telling themselves this probably was n't a bad election to lose . Why ? Because they could see consumer prices had taken off and had further to go . Using higher interest rates to get @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ , possibly inducing a recession . <p> Loading <p> This is why Dutton 's question is so seductive to people who do n't follow politics and the economy , and do n't want to use their grey matter . " If I felt the pain on your watch , it 's obvious you 're to blame and you get the sack . Do n't bother me with the details . " <p> Remember , however , that all the rich economies suffered the same inflation surge we did , all of them responded with higher interest rates , and most suffered rising unemployment and even , like the Kiwis , a recession . But not us . <p> So let me ask you a different question : over the past three years have you ever had cause to worry about losing your job ? Have you spent a lot of time unemployed while you find one ? Have more people in your house been able to find work ? <p> Our employment rate is higher than it 's ever been . Our rate of unemployment is still almost the lowest @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ because the Albanese government and the Reserve Bank agreed to get inflation down without a recession .

@@123078044 <h> Public opinion data , part 3 : Managing the obstacles <p> Our previous article explored the challenges that can make using public opinion data ( POD ) a rocky road , from concerns about politicisation and perceived bias to trade-offs in rigour and resources . But the good news is that these barriers are not insurmountable . Our research has identified best practices from public servants , political advisors , and social researchers who have extensive experience in using POD effectively in policymaking . Their insights offer practical strategies for integrating POD in a way that enhances decision-making while navigating the complexities of the political environment . <h> 1 . Get the foundations right <p> One thing was clear across the board : for POD to be effective , it must be credible , rigorous and transparent -- ensuring it is appropriately interpreted and trusted as an evidence source . <p> Credibility hinges on a clearly articulated purpose , the qualifications of the research team , and the entity commissioning the research , all of which signal that the study is designed and conducted by experts with integrity and @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ of research in areas such as sampling design , question framing , and data analysis , which determine whether insights are reliable and fit for purpose . <p> Transparency involves clearly reporting methods and survey limitations . It also extends to the decision-making processes that shape the research . <h> 2 . Frame research to generate actionable insights <p> Clearly defining the scope , purpose , and role of PODs alongside other evidence is key to maintaining impartiality and ensuring alignment with policy goals and broader evidence needs . This framing also helps shift the focus toward underlying attitudes and behaviours rather than agreement or disagreement , strengthening its value as an evidence source . <p> This is especially important when testing social licence or implementation mechanisms , where the focus should be on understanding experiences , concerns and needs . For example , if a policy goal is to increase vaccination uptake , POD should be designed to understand the factors influencing vaccination decisions rather than aiming to measure public approval of vaccines . While insights into public sentiment may emerge in the process , the focus remains on @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ <p> Similarly , when policy decisions themselves are still being shaped , POD should not be designed as a referendum on what is most popular but as a tool to explore public needs , lived experiences , and the trade-offs people are willing to accept . <p> The difference is nuanced , but it fundamentally shapes how POD is approached -- shifting it from a tool that gauges political sentiment to one that provides actionable insights for policy development . <h> 3 . Work closely with ministers ' offices <p> Collaborating with ministers ' staff early in the process helps ensure that POD is both policy-relevant and attuned to the broader political landscape . Defining the scope and parameters of POD in consultation with ministerial staff increases the likelihood that insights will be used effectively and helps assess the risk of politicisation . <p> Beyond collaboration , political awareness is key . Staying informed about shifting priorities , constraints , and political realities allows public servants to anticipate concerns and proactively align POD insights with policy windows . This does n't mean shaping research to fit a political agenda but @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ preparing viable alternative approaches when needed . <p> By embedding POD within real-world policy dynamics , public servants can strengthen its role in decision-making -- helping ensure that it is seen as a valuable tool rather than a political risk . <h> From rocky road to well-worn path <p> These three recommendations support a broader goal : shifting the culture around POD in policymaking . In an ideal future , POD would be embedded alongside other evidence inputs as a routine part of the decision-making process -- while recognising that its use will naturally vary across jurisdictions and portfolios . <p> As one public servant we spoke to put it , normalising and legitimising POD is a " muscle " that needs to be strengthened -- not just at an individual level but across organisations . This means building capability among public servants to use POD rigorously , role-modelling from senior leaders to normalise its use as an evidence source , and creating incentives that reinforce best practice . These recommendations , along with our practice note , are meant to be a conversation starter , a step toward embedding @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ straining the rocky road metaphor past breaking point , the territory ahead of Australia is treacherous and uncharted . The mega-trends that will shape the next few decades -- AI , climate change , the aging population , and so on -- will likely require fundamental systems change . The more deeply policymakers can understand the public -- their fears , beliefs , values , imperatives -- the better designed those systems will be , and the more robust social licence will be . <p> Public Opinion Data is a powerful tool that helps to chart the path . <p> Note : This series of articles was written by researchers from Monash Sustainable Development Institute , summarising the key insights from the research Bridging Public Opinion Data and Policy : A Mixed-Methods Analysis . The research was commissioned by ANZSOG and the Australian Public Service Commission ( APSC ) , as part of ANZSOG 's field-leading research model , which brings together public sector bodies with university researchers to address cutting edge problems in public administration .

@@123120923 <h> Cutting red tape is difficult <p> Playing the blame game over who is responsible for the current low economic growth in many rich countries has become a political norm . But at least on one issue , there seems to be a relatively broad consensus in most countries and across party lines : countries in the European Union , the United States , and other high-income countries such as Australia do not need more bureaucracy -- they need significantly less . <p> That may sound reasonable , but the demand to reduce bureaucracy is anything but new . Political leaders in the past have repeatedly struggled to reduce red tape , which begs the question : why is it so difficult ? <p> Certain bureaucratic regulations in democratic countries with representative governments were initially introduced with good reason -- or at least with good intentions . Often , their aim was to benefit society as a whole by reducing market failures . However , instead of enhancing welfare , many existing and newly introduced regulations are now seen as an unnecessary burden -- sometimes even as outright harassment . @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ up stifling both . <p> Some of the knowledge of which regulations are outdated or detrimental to public welfare largely rests with the employees of government administrations . Understandably , they have little incentive to streamline bureaucracy to the point where they risk making themselves redundant . Instead , they have an incentive to increase regulation as this gives them more budget and power , as discussed in the classical theory of bureaucracy . As a result , valuable insider knowledge on how to reduce bureaucracy remains largely untapped . <p> On top of that , some bureaucratic regulations were introduced purely for ideological reasons by political decision-makers . As a result , when it comes to reducing bureaucracy , politicians are , at best , willing to eliminate rules that contradict their own ideology -- while deeming their own regulations indispensable . Moreover , they tend to call for ad hoc new regulations in times of crisis . <p> For these reasons , many past attempts to reduce bureaucracy have failed . Therefore , it is essential that citizens , businesses , and even the administration itself actively strive @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ or allowing it to expand further . But how can bureaucracy be successfully reduced ? We propose a simple approach to bureaucratic reduction and regulatory reform that we call " Rules Against Rules . " <p> Institutional rules to cut red tape need to be few and simple . At the same time , they must be both broad and compelling -- so clear and logical that virtually no one could argue or object against them . They should not only be capable of securing majority support but should ideally be passed with near-unanimous approval . At the same time , these fundamental rules must be specific enough to ensure measurable and lasting progress in eliminating unnecessary regulations . In this context , we see particular potential in two key rules that could serve as guiding principles for reducing bureaucracy . <h> Rule 1 : No duplicate regulations <p> This rule states that once a specific regulation addresses a political objective , no additional regulations may be introduced to achieve the same goal . The principle is easy to understand , logical , and likely to receive substantial public support @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ significant reduction and simplification of bureaucracy . <p> A clear example of this issue can be found in environmental and climate policy with respect to the European Union . The European Union has established the Emissions Trading System ( EU-ETS ) as a key instrument for reducing CO2 emissions . Under the EU-ETS , regulatory emission caps create a CO2 price , which incentivizes profit-oriented companies to lower their emissions . The EU-ETS is already being used to reduce emissions successfully ; it will be expanded to cover buildings , road transport and further sectors such that , in the long run , it contributes to increasing welfare by reducing costs of climate change -- assuming that the rest of the world implements similar measures in the future . <p> Thus , additional regulations for climate protection , at least in the EU , can generally be considered duplicate regulations and , in line with Bureaucracy Reduction Rule 1 , should be abolished . Regulating beyond the welfare-optimal level set by the EU-ETS price mechanism is unnecessary and harmful . With climate regulations now permeating nearly every aspect of daily @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ is enormous . A particularly important step is the elimination of all climate-related documentation requirements unless they are essential for the proper functioning of emissions trading . Such documentation obligations often impose a disproportionate burden on businesses while rarely making a direct contribution to improving climate protection . Since there should be " no duplicate regulations " , there is enormous potential to cut unnecessary bureaucracy . <h> Rule 2 : If one government agency has the information , no other should ask for It again <p> This rule tackles a fundamental issue of bureaucracy : the excessive burden of redundant information requests on citizens and businesses . It is neither necessary nor efficient for government agencies to repeatedly ask for data that another authority already possesses . Instead , a binding mechanism should be implemented to enable seamless information exchange between government agencies , while ensuring explicit consent from individuals to uphold data protection and privacy standards . <p> Implementing this principle would also incentivise politicians to expand digital access to government services . Australia , for example , has successfully introduced myGov , a simple and secure platform @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ place . However , many other countries are lagging behind in adopting similar measures . There is significant potential to streamline bureaucratic processes and enhance efficiency through further digitalisation . <p> The rule " If One Government Agency Has the Information , No Other Should Ask for It Again " forces government agencies to significantly improve their efficiency , as retrieving information from various authorities requires considerable effort . Agencies would have to optimize their internal processes and workflows to systematically utilize the already available data . They would also be forced to complete most forms to a large degree themselves instead of burdening businesses and citizens . As a result , many documentation processes would either become fully automated or be rendered obsolete or superfluous . <p> Likewise , the rule foresees that information that government agencies already possess should not have to be separately documented again by citizens and businesses . If necessary , the administration can document it internally -- provided , of course , that the information is truly needed . And if an agency has to go through the effort of documenting itself , one @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ first place . <h> Enforcing the rules against bureaucracy <p> Ideally , the two core bureaucracy reduction rules should be legally enforceable in court . Citizens and businesses who believe they are subject to duplicate regulations should have the right to file lawsuits . This would actively leverage public knowledge to help eliminate unnecessary bureaucracy . At the same time , government agencies would be required to prove that specific regulations are truly necessary and do not constitute redundant regulation . Anticipating legal challenges to new rules , administrations would proactively work to avoid duplicate regulations . Before introducing any new regulation , agencies would be compelled to conduct a thorough internal review to ensure it does not simply regulate something that is already regulated . <p> Furthermore , government employees should be required to report suspected cases of duplicate regulations . Likewise , they should be obligated to flag situations where they believe another government agency already possesses the necessary information . This would foster natural skepticism and restraint within the administration when it comes to introducing new regulations and expanding bureaucracy . <p> By making these two fundamental @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ of potential violations , they would fully unfold their impact within the administration . <h> A role model for bureaucratic reduction <p> Instead of trying to cut regulation with a chainsaw or set up a new Department of Government Efficiency , which itself faces potential issues with oversight , our proposed bureaucracy reduction rules -- " No duplicate regulations " and " If one government agency has the information , no other should ask for it again " can be easily implemented by changes to existing legal codes or constitutions . <p> Both rules are likely to gain strong support from citizens , which will , over time , lead to widespread political backing . As fundamental principles , they face minimal legal obstacles but have the potential to significantly reduce bureaucracy where necessary while preserving essential regulations that benefit citizens . Rather than a somewhat reckless " chainsaw " approach or a " Wild West " deregulation frenzy , a systematic , orderly , and rule-based reduction of bureaucracy would be a welcome reform in most countries . It could enhance efficiency , improve governance , and ultimately make @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ such that they all would be great again . <h> Enjoying this complimentary article ? @@123145260 <h> Greener perspectives : Matthias Irger <p> Architects and designers are at the forefront of shaping not only how places look but also how they are built . For our third edition of Greener Perspectives , we spoke with Dr Matthias Irger , Head of Sustainability at Cox . Here 's what he had to say about his commitment to regenerative solutions and the importance of driving low-carbon solutions . <h> Architecture &amp; Design Team <p> Architects and designers are at the forefront of shaping not only how places look but also how they are built . For our third edition of Greener Perspectives , we spoke with Dr Matthias Irger , Head of Sustainability at Cox . Here 's what he had to say about his commitment to regenerative solutions and the importance of driving low-carbon solutions . <p> Can you share a brief overview of your journey and career in architecture and what drew you to focus on sustainability ? <p> I studied architecture and urban design in Germany , with an internship mid-way through in Sydney . After completing my degree , I began my career at @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ high-rises . Then in 2004 , I moved back to Sydney and joined Cox , marking the beginning of my journey with the firm . <p> After some years at Cox , I left to work on 8 Chifley Square -- a groundbreaking project at the time . It was Sydney 's first Six Star Green Star commercial office tower designed by RSHP , and I worked on it while at Lippmann Partnership . This deepened my passion for sustainable design and led me to pursue a PhD in Sustainable Urbanism , focusing on climate adaptation and urban heat mitigation . Eventually , I returned to Cox , where I 'm now Head of Sustainability . Coming to Australia 20 years ago , I noticed that sustainability standards were far lower here than I 'd experienced in Europe . That realisation was a pivotal moment for me -- it fuelled my determination to understand how we could lift the bar and improve outcomes , not just in architecture but across our cities . <p> How do you integrate sustainability into your day-to-day work and project designs ? <p> At Cox @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ 's part of our DNA . Philip Cox founded the company over 60 years ago with an environmentally conscious approach , and we continue to honour that legacy . It 's reflected in our studio values , like " create to last " and " do more with less " , which resonates deeply with our team and clients alike . Using fewer materials , reducing carbon , and creating durable , lasting buildings are key principles we follow . <p> As Head of Sustainability , I 'm involved in many projects across our studios , guiding our strategic direction on carbon reduction , material circularity , and building disassembly for end-of-life considerations . I also work closely with our teams through education and advice on improving design outcomes . <p> SBRC , Wollongong , NSW <p> Were there any pivotal moments or projects that significantly shaped your approach to sustainable architecture ? <p> A pivotal moment for me was realising the massive responsibility architects and planners hold in addressing climate change . The built environment contributes to about 30% of global carbon emissions -- 10-11% from the materials we @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ it clear that simply being " sustainable " is n't enough . We need to shift to regenerative design , creating buildings that are net positive and give back more than they take , especially as we 're consuming resources far beyond what the Earth can sustain . <p> One project that stands out is the Sustainable Buildings Research Centre ( SBRC ) at the University of Wollongong , Australia 's first certified Living Building . This project proved that net-positive buildings are achievable if approached correctly and supported by an ambitious client . <p> The SBRC excels in passive design -- artificial lighting is rarely needed , and air conditioning is unnecessary , creating a space where people feel healthier and more productive . The use of reclaimed materials like old timber and recycled brick adds warmth , comfort , and creates a sense of place . <p> This project inspired the establishment of the Living Future Institute in Australia and demonstrated how architecture can create spaces that positively impact both the planet and its occupants . It 's proof that sustainable , regenerative architecture is n't just aspirational @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ 's first and still only fully certified Living Building . The SBRC is net positive in energy and water , and was built with local , reclaimed materials such as brick and structural timber . <p> How does circularity influence your material selection and what challenges have you encountered in sourcing sustainable materials ? <p> Circularity is a core principle in our design approach , working alongside carbon reduction efforts . We focus on designing for disassembly by using mechanical fixings instead of glue , ensuring components can be reused or recycled . We prioritise materials with high recycled content and adaptive reuse , repurposing buildings or components rather than demolishing them , which helps reduce carbon emissions and waste while saving costs . <p> However , sourcing sustainable materials in Australia can be challenging due to a lack of transparency around carbon metrics and supply chain data . We often face the dilemma of choosing between local products without the necessary information and imported ones with certifications . To address this , we helped develop Product Aware , a database that gathers sustainability metrics for both local and international @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ the data we need . We hope this initiative encourages more local products to provide transparency and facilitates the transition to more sustainable alternatives , particularly in high-carbon materials like aluminium . <p> What role do you believe architects play in driving sustainable practices in the construction industry ? <p> Architects play a crucial role in the transition to a low-carbon economy . We 're responsible for a large portion of carbon emissions through the materials we choose , how we design buildings , and how we plan cities . As designers , we have a moral responsibility to act because we have the power to make a difference . Sustainable design is often simple , requiring skilful design rather than complex solutions . <p> With the right skills , we can create buildings that are both sustainable and efficient , offering benefits like lower energy costs , better health outcomes , and higher resale values at the end of their first life . On a city scale , we can make urban spaces more resilient to heat and flooding by integrating nature and improving liveability . <p> What are @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ your career ? <p> The most important lesson I 've learned is to think about sustainability from the very start of a project -- it 's a mindset . From the initial concept , we need to consider how to reduce the environmental footprint and aim for net-positive outcomes , not just sustainable ones . Understanding the site is crucial , especially considering climate change risks , and how we can mitigate those challenges . <p> Another key lesson is that sustainability does n't have to cost more . With passive design , like optimising windows , roof overhangs , and thermal mass , we can reduce costs by saving energy in the long run . Investing in better insulation , air tightness , and glazing upfront leads to long-term savings and a more valuable building . <p> How do you foresee sustainability shaping the future of architecture and urban design over the next five years ? <p> Sustainability will gain more prominence , with a major focus on carbon and climate risk . The shift from traditional design to actually quantifying carbon will be a game changer . Once @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ , and benchmark our designs , making real progress . AI-supported optimisation tools will also transform the design process , making it more efficient and making designers ' lives easier . <p> What advice would you give to architects and designers who want to start prioritising sustainability throughout their projects where there may be resistance from clients etc. ? <p> My advice would be to think about sustainability in everything you do , no matter how small . Every design choice , whether it 's using fewer materials or selecting sustainable alternatives , has an impact . Continually look at successful projects for inspiration and learn from past mistakes . And finally , do n't forget the basics -- understanding the site , optimising solar design , and using technology can make a big difference . It 's all about making small , thoughtful decisions that add up over time .

@@123163057 <h> Get the SBS Audio app <h> Other ways to listen <h> Climate adaptation refers to the process of adjusting to the actual or projected effects of climate change and ensuring vulnerable communities are well-equipped for disaster . But some experts say the term has been reduced to nothing more than a political talking point . A new report by researchers at Monash University shows little action has been taken to prepare at-risk communities over the past decade , despite disaster events occurring more frequently and at a higher intensity . <p> That question was considered at length at the United Nations Climate Change Conference , COP-13 , in 2007 . <p> There , the international community came to understand that climate adaptation is just as important as mitigation . <p> Dr Simon Bradshaw , a fellow with the Climate Council and director at Climate-KIC Australia , explains . <p> " In responding to climate change , there 's really two key tasks . First and most important is we 've got to get our greenhouse gas emissions down as fast as possible by moving beyond fossil fuels . That @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ That 's essential to limiting future harms . We 're already seeing a real acceleration in the impacts of climate change and worsening fire seasons , more destructive storms and downpours . Now , the second thing we have to do at the same time is adapt and build our resilience and learn to cope with these various impacts . " <p> A year later , in 2008 , the federal government initiated the National Climate Change Adaptation Research Facility to develop the knowledge decision-makers needed to effectively adapt Australia to the impacts of climate change . <p> But its findings are yet to be translated into action . <p> That lag is reflected in a new report by researchers at Monash University . <p> It found local action on climate adaptation remains insufficient across tiers of government , with little change over the decade between 2012 to 2022 . <p> He says those who have experienced bushfires , coastal erosion , flooding and drought want to help create adaptation measures . <p> " The governance structures were n't there , the finance was n't there , the means of @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ actually act on that information , you need to have the capacity to act , you need to have the governance regime at a local level to act , and you need to have access to the funds to actually implement that action . " <p> A second study , by researchers at the University of New South Wales , has found disaster recovery is being delayed by a lack of strategy . <p> Lead researcher and inaugural Judith Neilson Chair in Architecture at the University of New South Wales , Professor David Sanderson , says top-down bureaucracy has stifled any meaningful effort . <p> " This is a global evidence truth that the best recovery is as localised as possible . But we have in Australia and elsewhere systems which are largely top down and the sweet spot is supporting recovery of communities rather than , if you like , directing from afar . That 's a quick summary of a complex story , but what we 've noticed in our research -- and again in pretty much every country -- local governments are tasked with a lot of @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ but yet are woefully under-resourced . " <p> He also says short-term solutions are wasteful and rob vulnerable communities of the chance to build resilience in the face of climate change . <p> " A kneejerk political reaction -- it often is to think quick , we need to build temporary housing after a disaster and that 's all over the place . But the problem with temporary housing is it 's slow , it 's expensive , and there 's really a plan for what to do afterwards . So , we 're arguing that temporary housing , if you build it , is an absolute last resort . There may be arguably a case for it , but a last resort and there must be a plan for its investment in continuation afterwards . There must be a plan for its investment in continuation afterwards so it 's a valuable asset to the community . " <p> The shortfall in strategy has also accelerated cost-of-living pressures . <p> The Treasury 's Intergenerational Report pointed to the escalating costs of natural disasters borne by taxpayers , which reached $7 @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ costs are reflected in insurance policies and in other ways that are less immediately detectable . <p> " Natural disasters , which have a very dramatic impacts and you 're seeing the impact of that in your insurance policies . In the last quarterly CPI , insurance was one of the biggest areas of increase in terms of cost of living . But the slow burn is in things like health and mental health , and we tend to not take as much notice of those areas because they 're very slow , but cumulatively they can be just as severe if not more severe than the natural disaster impact . " <p> A 2023 Climate Trauma study by the Climate Council found 80 per cent of Australians experienced some form of disaster at least once since 2019 . <p> One reason for that , Dr Bradshaw says , is houses are being zoned and built in high-risk areas . <p> " It 's fair to say that updates to planning regulations have just not kept up with the increasing impacts of climate change , be that flood risk or @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ some improvements here , some re-zoning , some restrictions on building in particularly flood prone areas . But we do still have new developments being built on flood plains and we still have an enormous number of our houses built in places where people are inevitably going to face real difficulty in future . " <p> While stressing urgency , Dr Spencer says the way adaption efforts are approached needs to be more holistic , pointing to what he calls " district modelling " . <p> " Climate impacts do n't respect jurisdiction . They will cross jurisdictions of local government , they 'll involve the catchment management authority , they 'll involve the chamber of commerce . Voters should know if their money was spent on town hall meetings where their voice could be heard , or if it funded a petty smear campaign on social media . <p> The present funding model simply props up the entitled professional political class . No wonder voters are more disillusioned and disengaged than ever . @@123164331 <h> The world 's most powerful ocean current could slow by 2050 <p> Banner : Supplied <p> New research finds the more Antarctic ice melts , the more the ocean is flooded by melt water , the more the Antarctic Circumpolar Current is likely to slow down -- creating a vicious climate change cycle <p> You may already be familiar with some of the features of the meridional overturning circulation -- there 's the Gulf Stream along the east coast of the United States or the East Australian Current , which regulates ocean temperatures between Brisbane and the south coast of New South Wales . <p> But there 's also a much less well-known behemoth of a current that sits just to Australia 's south . <p> It 's called the Antarctic Circumpolar Current ( ACC ) and it 's enriched with eddies and jets . It flows around Antarctica and connects our planet 's three major ocean basins -- the Pacific , Atlantic and Indian Oceans . <p> The ACC is more than 100 times stronger than the current of the Amazon River and five times stronger than the @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ separates the Antarctic continent from its northern neighbours , acting as a physical and oceanographic barrier that isolates the icy continent . <p> Slide to see the modelling of the decline of ACC from 2010 to 2050 . Graphic : Supplied <p> Given its power , any changes are likely to have an impact on the health of the Antarctic continent -- but are also likely to affect our global climate . <p> Over the years , there has been a lot of scientific debate about the impact of climate change on the ACC . <p> Although recent research has shown that the ACC 's strength has n't changed significantly , the impact of Antarctica 's melting ice is less well understood by the science . So our team designed a new model to look more closely at its impact . <p> Schematic of changing Southern Ocean zonal transport and its link to ocean overturning and stratification . Arrows show the transport in the RYF and future simulations , and curly arrows mark changes to deep convection . Graphic : Supplied <p> Because this strong current surrounds Antarctica , it @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ this pristine continent . <p> If the ACC were to weaken , it may allow the migration of warmer water towards Antarctica , which would cause more ice to melt and slow the current even more -- creating a vicious cycle . <p> And with that warm water comes the potential for migrating invasive species like the Southern Bull Kelp to reach Antarctica , disturbing the delicate food web there -- something the ACC may currently help to prevent , <p> Beyond the local impacts of an ACC slowdown , there are also the global repercussions . <h> Follow Pursuit <p> Social media <h> Acknowledgement of country <p> We acknowledge Aboriginal and Torres Strait Islander people as the Traditional Owners of the unceded lands on which we work , learn and live . But human-caused climate change is warming Australia and surrounding oceans at an unnatural pace , changing our weather patterns and modifying the structure and moisture content of the atmosphere . <p> These all ultimately lead to changes in the occurrence and intensity of many extreme weather events . <p> We can expect heatwaves to get hotter and longer , extreme rainfall from thunderstorms should get heavier and fire weather days are likely to increase in number . <p> These changes depend on location and scientists have more confidence in trends for some extremes compared to others . Nonetheless , there is high confidence that the ' new normal ' is more extreme than the old one . <p> It is possible to determine whether a specific extreme event or group of events , like those many of us are experiencing now , are made more likely or more intense by climate change . <p> The process is called ' event attribution ' and it typically requires detailed data analysis after the fact , a well-developed scientific understanding of the impact @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ capability . <p> Large parts of the nation 's north faced severe flooding , with some areas recording more than a metre of rain . What we can say with confidence is that the new normal will feature high-impact weather events that test our resilience to climate change . <p> As these extremes play out , they highlight some of our future societal challenges . <p> In the coming years , we will break more heatwave records , especially in cities . These strategies aim to lower fire intensity and rate of spread by simplifying fuels <p> Suppression focuses on controlling and containing fires once they start , as well as protecting assets like buildings , roads and powerlines by deploying people , fire trucks and aircraft to slow or stop the fires and in turn reduce damage . <p> But neither approach alone is a silver bullet . <p> Fuel management requires careful planning and is often constrained by weather conditions , public perception and considerations of key trade-offs @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ of fire management <p> Our research explored this problem for regions in Victoria by combining climate data , fire simulations and cost data to develop a framework for evaluating the cost-effectiveness of various fire management strategies now and into the future . <p> We developed a model designed to capture uncertainty and evaluate the outcomes of hypothetical fire management strategies under varying climate scenarios . <p> This approach enabled us to analyse data from over 1,200 fire regime simulations , covering 16 modelled management strategies across six regions and six climate models . <p> This meant we could characterise a range of potential future outcomes and evaluate them against one another for current and future conditions . <p> As the climate continues to warm , even the best strategies face mounting challenges . These strategies varied significantly between regions , but generally reduced wildfire impacts more efficiently than doing nothing or the most intensive interventions ( i.e. throwing everything we have at it ) . <p> Doing nothing is not a cost-effective option . <p> Under current and worsening climate conditions , the cost of inaction was consistently higher than any management strategy . <p> These costs are all impacts on societal values and the environment . @@123164337 <p> Australia must do more to empower communities of colour in its response to climate change . <p> In late February , the Multicultural Leadership Initiative hosted its Our Common Future summits in Sydney and Melbourne . These summits focused on the importance of multicultural climate advocacy , the disproportionate impact of climate change on people of colour and the need to build climate resilience at a grassroots level . <p> These summits brought together a range of First Nations , Pasifika , people of colour , and culturally and linguistically diverse advocates and stakeholders . The need for a conference of this nature is clear : although climate change threatens us all , people of colour are often marginalised within mainstream climate-change discourse . As highlighted by Minister for Climate Change Chris Bowen in his keynote speech at the Sydney summit , we need to dispel the myth that climate change is only ' a concern for inner-city Anglo-Celtic elites ' . <p> The inclusion of people of colour in this conversation is an ethical imperative , as climate change often disproportionately affects people of colour . In Western @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ population speaks a language other than English at home and the proportion of low-income earners is higher than the rest of Sydney . This area is typically six to 10 degrees hotter than the rest of the city during extreme heat events . These events therefore pose a significant challenge to low-income migrants with English as a second language , who often lack access to quality healthcare and housing . <p> This is also evident in developing countries . Although the Global South contributes a relatively small amount to global greenhouse gas emissions , these countries are on the frontline of climate change . One only has to look at international headlines to see the severity of climate disasters , including floods in South Asia and rising sea levels in Pacific island countries such as Tuvalu . <p> These are not one-off events . They are emblematic of a broader trend of climate injustice : rich , developed countries are doing relatively little to respond to climate events , despite contributing more to climate change . At COP26 in 2021 , many African voices were underrepresented due to limited funding and difficulty securing Covid-19 vaccines , both of which were necessary for in-person participation . @@123190745 <p> The Hunga Tonga volcanic eruption of January 2022 was expected to warm the planet , as hundreds of millions of tonnes of water vapour was injected into the atmosphere . But it did n't according to US researchers . <p> Hunga Tonga-Hunga Ha'apai is a submarine volcano , with a vent 200m below the ocean 's surface . It sits 20o south of the Equator ( Sydney is 33oS ) , on the boundary of the Pacific and Indo-Australian tectonic plates , about 65km north of Tongatapu , Tonga 's main island . The small islands projecting above sea level were uninhabited prior to the eruption but are known for their guano deposits . <p> Being underwater complicates the effect of eruptions on climate . " Large volcanic eruptions near the equator that eject a lot of sulphate aerosols generally have a cooling effect on the atmosphere " CSIRO climate scientist , Dr Michael Grose told Cosmos . <p> Sulphur dioxide gas ejected by volcanoes combines with water vapour in the atmosphere to form sulphates , tiny particles , which physically block sunlight , reducing temperatures . NASA says that heating in that year was 0.89oC above the average for their baseline 1951-1980 . ( Since then , 2024 has been confirmed as the hottest year on record , at 1.5oC above pre-industrial levels . ) <p> But researchers found a net cooling effect of about 0.1oC in the Southern Hemisphere , by the end of 2022 and 2023 , despite the eruption of " unprecedented amounts " of water vapor into the stratosphere , says lead author , Gupta . <p> Gupta concluded that because sulphate particles in this eruption were 50% smaller than those of Pinatubo , they may have been better at blocking sunlight , despite the heavy water vapour load . " <p> These results have a much broader context . Geoengineering , altering the global climate to prevent catastrophic climate change , has included discussion of approaches such as injecting sulphate aerosols into the atmosphere to counteract global heating . <p> " If we plan to use approaches that involve releasing sulphate aerosols into the stratosphere to reflect sunlight , we have to consider how other factors -- such as water vapor and atmospheric mixing -- could change the outcome , " says Gupta . <p> " The overall impact of such measures depends on understanding the complex interactions among atmospheric components that affect the formation and properties of stratospheric sulphate aerosols . @@123191022 <p> One of the worst habits of Australia 's political journalists is angrily demanding economic modelling of climate policies and then blankly refusing to interrogate them . The requested presence of a big PDF provides a neat little escape from thinking critically about a problem like climate change , a crisis truly unsuited to the habits and desires of political journalism . <p> There is a long-running precedent for engaging with climate through the economic modelling frame . Ahead of the 2019 federal election , a weary Bill Shorten was hounded by then Channel Ten ( now Sky News Australia ) reporter Jonathan Lea , who demanded to see " costings " for Labor 's emissions reduction target of 45% by 2030 . Lea 's questions triggered a sort of flocking behaviour from other journalists and a slew of articles admonishing Labor for not " costing " its policy . <p> Fast forward six years and the ABC 's David Speers is worried that Peter Dutton has n't released any detail on his claim that reserving gas domestically and opening up a raft of new gas fields will bring down @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ let alone any modelling , to explain exactly how this ' gas reservation ' policy will work " . Shadow energy minister Ted O'Brien has been hounded , repeatedly , on when the Coalition will release its modelling . <p> Everyone needs to take a pause and ask why exactly we want to see an 80-page PDF filled with charts , numbers and jargon . Is it a meaningful or useful window into the way that climate policies manifest in human society ? What the hell do you get out of that document ? <p> As the Australia Institute 's Richard Denniss wrote a decade ago , the entire concept of economic modelling is deeply flawed . <p> In most cases , economic modelling is n't used to help us understand the costs and benefits of major projects or policy changes . It is used to conceal them . Rather than outline and discuss the wide range of winners and losers , debate the pros and cons , and make transparent decisions , economic modelling allows all of the messy bits to be hidden . <p> What is clear from @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ false precision and faux-empiricism . <p> The way it works -- and the way it 'll work with Dutton 's gas modelling -- is a PDF is emailed around to journalists who are both unwilling and incapable of interrogating the underlying assumptions and calculations . The big headlines ( " COALITION GAS POLICY WILL CUT GAS COSTS BY $200 BILLION " , or something ) are put online and printed on paper before the first sip of morning coffee -- and well before any actual expert can pick it apart . <p> When modelling is done right , it 's presented with care and caveats : huge error bars reflecting the inherent uncertainty of the future dominate presentation . But that is rarely how it plays out . After modelling is demanded by journalists and provided by politicians , it spawns furious debates , each jailed narrowly in the cage imagined by the modellers . <p> The Coalition 's modelling of its nuclear policy , for instance , was written by Frontier Economics , shared as a PDF , and came packed with a bunch of wild assumptions ( such @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ It has spawned endlessdiscourse around whether the modelling accurately reflects the real costs of capping renewable energy and relying on fossil gas and nuclear power . <p> But all this is taking place after the Coalition spent almost a decade doing literally nothing to legalise nuclear power in Australia , with zero real signs it would do anything different if elected . Climate critics and advocates alike ended up debating the narrow specifics of something that simply wo n't ever happen . That 's the cage at work . <p> Labor 's oft-repeated promise to cut power bills by precisely $275 by 2025 was drawn from modelling by Reputex , published at the end of 2021 . The gas-induced power price crisis obviously played a major role in denying that eventuality , but it 's worth noting that renewable energy in the National Electricity Market is also far lower than what Reputex assumed it would be : 39% at the end of 2024 , rather than just above 50% as assumed in its 2021 report . <p> That is really a material difference : <p> While Labor 's " Capacity @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ into renewable energy construction , it did n't come soon enough to maintain the industry 's rapid pace during the latter years of the renewable energy target scheme . That delay caused a dip in new clean energy in the middle of Labor 's first term , and a stagnation in the once-rapid increase in clean energy percentage in Australia 's grid ( and the first systemic rise in power grid emissions since the Abbott years ) . <p> This is interesting . @@123202656 <h> John Hewson Memories from the campaign trail <p> The launch of the campaign for the May 3 federal election brings back many memories , laughs and cautionary tales of my experiences on the trail in the 1990s . <p> As opposition leader , I had embarked on a big-picture strategy . @@123202673 <h> Tim Flannery A coalition of climate vandals <p> As a scientist , I 've watched climate change be kicked around Australia 's parliament like a political football for decades , with mounting frustration . It 's a history marked by denial , distraction and delay -- and Australians are already paying dearly for the failure of former governments to take climate change seriously . <p> When the last federal election rolled around in 2022 , Australia was a global climate pariah , following nine years of negligence under Liberal -- National governments . Australia had one of the weakest climate targets among developed countries . We had no credible policies to cut climate pollution or reach net zero . Renewable power investment had stalled , climate science had been cut , and our reputation on the world stage was in shreds . <p> Thankfully , Australians voted for change . That election marked a critical turning point for climate politics in Australia , where voters rejected years of polluting policies and elected a parliament with a clear mandate to take stronger action on climate . <p> We 've finally @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ Australia 's national grid is powered by renewables such as solar and wind , backed up by big batteries and hydro . Last year one in 10 new vehicles sold in Australia was electric , and we finally have limits on climate pollution for new cars . In the past three years under the Albanese government , Australia has adopted a binding ( albeit still too low ) 2030 climate target , set stricter limits on big industrial polluters and unlocked billions of dollars of investment in clean energy . <p> Shortly after his election victory , Prime Minister Anthony Albanese told the BBC that his government had " an opportunity now to end the climate wars " . With the Coalition having lost many of its inner-city seats to pro-climate independents , Australians could be forgiven for thinking they had sent both major parties a clear message on climate . <p> Delaying climate action might sound less sinister than denying it outright , but the impacts are just as dangerous ... Years of policy chaos under former Coalition governments have left Australians more exposed . <p> The fight is @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ taken on a more insidious form . Where some political leaders once denied climate science outright , now they hide behind a fa ? ade of false solutions , misleading claims and distractions . <p> There is no better example of this than the federal Coalition 's climate and energy policies today . Peter Dutton emerged from the last election as an opposition leader walking a political tightrope between voters who were horrified by the Black Summer bushfires and clamouring for climate action , and a party room still gripped by climate denial , repulsed by renewables and clinging to a toxic relationship with coal and gas . <p> Dutton had the chance to face this challenge head-on : to do the hard work of bringing his party 's policies in line with the concerns of everyday Australians who want genuine climate action ; by embracing renewable power @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ pollution to protect our children 's future . Yet the Coalition still insists its nuclear scheme is credible , because it could , in theory , provide zero-emissions power once it is up and running in the 2040s . Scientists are clear the lion 's share of cuts to climate pollution must occur now -- in the 2020s . <p> So here we see the new face of climate denial in Australia : delay and obstruction . <p> The Trojan Horse of the Coalition 's nuclear scheme became clear last week , when Dutton dusted off former prime minister Scott Morrison @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ the gas industry , which would plug gaps in our energy system while Australians wait decades for nuclear . <p> The science is clear : to avoid the worst impacts of climate change , there can be no new or expanded coal , oil or gas developments . To continue spending public money on prolonging fossil fuels is climate vandalism but exactly what we 've come to expect from a Coalition that has spent decades undermining climate action . <p> Whereas the Abbott government scrapped Australia 's carbon price , Dutton 's opposition voted against every bill to act on climate change in this term of parliament . Now , the Coalition wants to cut support for new transmission projects , wind back the New Vehicle Efficiency Standard and rip out the foundations of Australia 's clean energy transformation . By Romy Ash . <h> Richard Roxburgh on the job of an actor <p> Actor and director Richard Roxburgh first met Peter Greste over sandwiches during pre-production for The Correspondent . The film , which opens this month and in which Roxburgh plays Greste , is based on The First Casualty , a memoir depicting the Australian war correspondent 's headline-making incarceration in a Cairo prison in the last days of 2013 . <p> " If you 're playing someone , it 's a huge privilege to have them in the room , " says Roxburgh of their meeting , which took place in the home of producer and former foreign correspondent Carmel Travers . " I was really conscious of that . I was immediately scanning him and studying him , just in a way that I guess actors do . Not that this was going to be , in any way , an exercise in mimicry or even attempting his @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ his internal landscape , his internal struggles , the horror , the building sense of horror that went with being arrested so strangely , as he was , just filling in for a friend over Christmas in Egypt , which was a place he 'd never been to as a journalist before . But it was still really important to me to get the measure of him . " <p> Greste not only tells his own story -- he contextualises it in what he calls " a global war on journalism " . Greste was arrested in 2013 with his Al Jazeera colleagues , Egyptian -- Canadian producer Mohamed Fahmy and local cameraman Baher Mohamed . The subsequent incarceration occurred at a tense political time , after Abdel Fattah el-Sisi 's military takeover of the democratically elected Egyptian government . This tense environment was in stark contrast to the domestic setting where Roxburgh met Greste . <p> For Roxburgh , the job of an actor is about trying , as much as possible , to actualise in his own imagination the experiences of the characters he plays . Over his @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ , he has approached many different roles . In Hollywood he played the villain Count Dracula in Van Helsing as a pompous , glam-rock bloodsucker . After this production , Roxburgh married one of Dracula 's three vampire brides , Italian actor Silvia Colloca . " The first thing she ever said to me -- because I had three brides , one Spanish , one American , one Italian -- the very first words she ever said to me were : ' Hi Richard , I 'm your Italian wife , ' ? " he says . " Which sure enough , came to pass , in due time . " He laughs as he retells the story of their meeting , a delightful , well-rehearsed bit of entertainment gossip that underlies their two decades of marriage . <p> " Whether you 're hitting journalists with bullets and shrapnel ... or subjecting them to threats or ridicule ... it 's all coming from the same place , which is about delegitimising truth . " <p> Roxburgh played Sherlock Holmes in The Hound of Baskervilles , his nemesis Professor Moriarty in @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ : Impossible 2 . Among his many roles in television is the lead in the hugely successful Australian drama Rake . His theatre roles , often with Sydney Theatre Company , include Estragon in Samuel Beckett 's Waiting for Godot and Vanya in Anton Chekhov 's Uncle Vanya . <p> Vanya , Roxburgh says , was demanding . " It was with this fabulous Hungarian director who was ... he 'd become the kind of audacious new voice of Chekhov , and he came as a package , because he could n't speak any English at all , so he worked with this fabulous woman called Anna , " he tells me . " He would speak in Hungarian and she would translate for him , for all of us . She was always beaming and effusive and wonderful and he was very deadpan -- speaking just in Hungarian . We would rehearse these scenes and he would start speaking at the end of it , and she would translate , and the translations that would come out were really quite brutal . <p> " ? ' This is appalling @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ ' I can not believe you have reached this point in your career , and you think this is okay , to perform a scene with this level of banality , ' ? " Roxburgh remembers . " So this translation was coming through -- I thought it was hilarious , and just wonderful ... because he was n't being mean , he was just being tough . @@123238805 <p> Australia 's agriculture sector and food system have prospered under a global rules-based system influenced by Western liberal values . But the assumptions , policy approaches and economic frameworks that have traditionally supported Australia 's food security are no longer fit for purpose . <p> Australia and the Indo-Pacific now face chronic challenges : rising geopolitical tensions , geo-economic transitions , climate change , deteriorating water security and rapid technological advances . While the government is acting to improve the Australian Defence Force 's readiness for conflict in our region , we are not trying to replicate this preparedness elsewhere in a coordinated manner , including in our agriculture sector and food system . <p> The importance of food security to national security , as well as policy options to resolve our national vulnerabilities , are core issues within ASPI 's newly released National Food Security Preparedness Green Paper . <p> The green paper argues that food is a fundamental pillar of Australia 's national security and the stability and security of the Indo-Pacific . The role of food in maintaining national security , as well as Australian and @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ and defence circles for long enough . Australia 's deteriorating strategic environment and critical dependencies on vulnerable supply chains mean we must now reassess our food security and consider its effects on Australian security and regional stability . <p> Australia is a heavily trade-dependent nation that exports 70 percent of its food production while facing an insidious domestic food insecurity challenge . Access to export markets is vital for all agriculture and food system stakeholders to maintain profitability . But , for decades , Australia has offshored the manufacturing of critical industry inputs in the name of globalisation and on the assumption that the world will remain in the rules-based order . Australia depends on many imported critical inputs , including fuel , AdBlue ( to reduce diesel emissions ) , fertiliser and , increasingly , labour . <p> Heightening regional trade and military tensions threaten Australia 's access to critical food system inputs and global markets . The Australian government is clear on the threats that we face . Australia can no longer rely on the traditional 10-year strategic warning time for conflict . Lifting Australia 's ability to @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ defence and expanding national resilience . <p> For food security , our problem is two-fold : Australia relies on vulnerable agricultural and food system supply chains , and , compounding the issue , does n't understand this vulnerability . It therefore has no clear plans for mitigation . <p> As shown in the figure below , since the 2008 global financial crisis , at least 20 academic papers , reports and inquiries have highlighted the importance of Australia 's food system and its exposure to external shocks . <p> Timeline of Australian food system reports . <p> Despite these reports , food security has not been a national priority , resulting in limited policy responses . <p> The Covid-19 pandemic revealed the scale of Australia 's exposure to long and fragile supply chains and the extent to which shocks to the international system could disrupt them . <p> Many disruptions have happened since then , with varying domestic effect . At the time of writing , yet another flood disaster is unfolding in regional Queensland , killing 150,000 head of livestock and counting . This disaster will have immense long-term @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ food production capacity . This follows the emptying of supermarket shelves in areas affected by Cyclone Alfred a month ago . There are also recurring Avian Influenza outbreaks in southern Australia . <p> On 4 March , the government committed to developing a National Food Security Strategy if re-elected . This is a starting point that has at least flagged food security as a specific policy priority . It appears likely that the opposition will support this initiative in some form . Regardless of what the next government looks like after the 3 May election , it must back this National Food Security Strategy with immediate action . <p> Australia must think of its agriculture and food system as an interconnected food security ecosystem , as opposed to a fragmented supply chain . Similarly , the importance of food security at a departmental and ministerial level must be elevated as a national security priority . @@123257968 <p> In some regions of the world , including parts of Africa , Asia , Americas and Australia , the conditions are right for megastorms to form . <p> These weather systems , known as " Mesoscale Convective Systems " ( MSCs ) , span thousands of square kilometres and are accompanied by extreme weather conditions , such as destructive winds , lightning , flash flooding and hail . <p> According to Dr Emma Barton , a meteorologist at the UK Centre for Ecology &amp; Hydrology : " MSCs are some of the most intense thunderstorms on the planet , and they are increasing in severity due to climate change . " <p> Barton is first author of a new study in Nature Geoscience , which has identified a new driver of larger megastorms : soil moisture . <p> By analysing satellite data collected from 2000-2019 , Barton and her collaborators discovered that soil moisture can alter atmospheric conditions , and subsequent storm size and rainfall in West Africa , India , South America , South Africa , Australia and the US Great Plains . <p> Specifically , large contrasts @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ atmospheric temperature gradients and leads to stronger shifts in wind direction and or speed higher up in the atmosphere . This favours larger storms that produce more rainfall . <p> This increase in rain ranges from 10 to 30% depending on the region and size of the storm . <p> " Rising temperatures could increase the contrast between wet and dry areas of soils , further intensifying thunderstorms in already severely impacted regions , " says Barton . <p> A storm in Rwanda . Credit : Cornelia Klein <p> Additional analysis of West Africa , India , South Africa and South America , which had sufficient storm data , revealed the surface soil conditions which strengthen these storms are present for 2 -- 5 days before they hit . <p> Integrating satellite observations of soil moisture into forecasting could improve advance warning of potential hazards such as flash flooding . The researchers say this will be particularly important in " data-sparse and climatically exposed regions such as Africa , where 60% of the population currently lack early warning systems . " <p> " Understanding how soil moisture influences storm activity @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ will be essential for more accurate short-term forecasting to warn communities about approaching storms , as well as making longer-term projections , " Barton says . <p> However , the researchers caution that the strength of the relationship between soil moisture and storm properties is likely different for each region . <p> " Therefore , the potential improvement in forecasting that can be achieved by accounting for surface conditions will also vary by region , " they write . <p> The next step is to explore what factors contribute to these regional variations .

The loss and damage fund was created at COP28 , acknowledging that developing nations are on the front lines of the climate crisis despite contributing the least . <p> The Climate Council states that COP is a world trade show highlighting what countries are doing to make progress . <p> Currently , there are two contenders to host COP31 -- Australia and Turkey . @@123309822 <p> So we 've asked some energy experts what they think are some of the solutions to help households now , and what are the long-term fixes Australia should focus on . <h> How we got here <p> Power prices have gone up significantly over the past few years , in a large part due to the war in Ukraine , kicking off a massive spike in the price of fossil fuels that drove coal and gas prices up around the globe , and at home . <p> While gas only plays a small part in Australia 's total power generation , it 's used at times when there 's lots of demand and is responsible for spikes in the wholesale electricity price . <p> More recently , Australia 's unreliable coal-fired power stations and a lack of transmission lines have also driven up prices . <p> Australia 's coal-fired power stations are reaching the end of their life cycle , so renewable energy is increasingly powering our grid , according to Dylan McConnell , an energy expert at the University of New South Wales . <p> " One thing @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ we already have .
